content.headline: Effect of Intravenous Carboplatin on Pain Control in Dogs with Appendicular Osteosarcoma
content.tagline: Help us study how carboplatin can help manage pain in dogs with bone cancer.
content.description: This study looks at whether a chemotherapy drug called carboplatin can help reduce pain in dogs that have osteosarcoma (bone cancer) in a leg. The researchers want to see if this medication improves how well dogs walk, how active they are during the day, and how well they sleep after treatment.
content.requirements:
1. Dogs will receive one intravenous (IV) dose of carboplatin on Day 0.
  2. Before treatment and once a week for 3 weeks, dogs will have:
  3. An orthopedic exam
  4. Walking tests using a force plate (to measure how well they walk)
  5. An activity monitor placed on their collar
  6. X-rays of the affected leg will be taken before treatment and again on Day 21.
  7. Blood tests will be done on Days 14 and 21.
  8. All study visits must take place at Colorado State University (CSU).
content.who_can_participate:
Dogs may participate if they:

  1. Have a confirmed diagnosis of osteosarcoma in a leg
  2. Dogs that are limping but still able to put weight on the affected leg
  3. Have acceptable blood test results
  4. Have not received chemotherapy or radiation before
  5. Have not taken certain bone medications within the last 30 days
  6. Dogs who have been on the same oral pain medications for at least 7 days
  7. Do not have evidence that the cancer has spread to other bones
  8. Can come to CSU for all study-related visits
content.benefits_and_risks:
Benefits

  1. The study covers many costs, including:
  2. Diagnostic tests before enrollment (blood work, urine tests, chest and leg X-rays, and tumor sampling)
  3. One carboplatin treatment
  4. Follow-up visits, X-rays, and blood tests
  5. Anti-nausea and anti-diarrhea medications initially provided for possible chemotherapy side effects 
  6. The study may help improve pain control for dogs with bone cancer.
  7. Information from the study may help future dogs with osteosarcoma.


Risks

  1. Dogs may experience side effects from chemotherapy, such as nausea or diarrhea.
  2. Blood draws and IV treatment may cause mild discomfort.
  3. Owners are responsible for extra medical costs if side effects require additional care beyond what the study provides.
content.compensation: This study will cover diagnostic tests, one carboplatin treatment, follow-up visits, radiographs, blood tests, anti-nausea and anti-diarrhea medications
content.responsibilities:
1. Bring their dog to all scheduled study visits at CSU.
  2. Make sure the dog wears the activity monitor at all times.
  3. Keep a simple log of activities, such as trips to the dog park, including the date and time.
  4. Pay for:
  5. Standard pain control medication for 7 days prior to starting study (Ex: Carprofen) 
  6. Any additional treatment costs if the dog has chemotherapy side effects beyond the initial medications provided by the study
